text: Your baby may start pulling up to stand using furniture. Make sure anything they grab onto is sturdy enough to support their weight.

Your baby's grasp is getting more precise. Toward 8-9 months, the pincer grasp — picking up small objects between thumb and forefinger — begins to emerge. Offer small, safe finger foods to encourage this skill.
Your baby may start "cruising" — walking while holding onto furniture. Arrange furniture close enough together that they can move between pieces.
Waving bye-bye, clapping, and pointing are all emerging social gestures around this age. Model these often and celebrate when your baby joins in.
Your baby understands more words than they can say. They may look at the dog when you say "dog" or glance at the door when they hear "outside."
Separation anxiety often peaks around 8-9 months. Quick, confident goodbyes work better than long, drawn-out ones. Your baby will adjust.
Your baby may start banging objects together, which shows they're learning to use both hands in coordination. Offer blocks, spoons, or cups to bang.
"Mama" or "dada" may emerge around now, though your baby might not use them specifically for you yet. Respond with excitement anyway!
Your baby may start understanding simple instructions like "give me the ball" or "where's your cup?" Use short, clear phrases and repeat often.
Crawling styles vary widely: traditional crawling, army crawling, scooting on their bottom, or even rolling. All are normal ways to get moving.
Your baby is becoming a little problem-solver. They may pull a blanket to get a toy on it or move an obstacle out of their way.
Imitation is in full swing. Your baby watches you closely and may try to "talk" on a phone, brush their hair, or wipe a surface like they've seen you do.
Some babies skip crawling entirely and go straight to pulling up and cruising. If your baby is finding their own way to move, they're doing great.
Your baby may start showing a preference for one hand over the other. True handedness develops later, but early preferences are normal.
Try showing your baby a simple cause-and-effect toy, like pressing a button to make a character pop up. The surprise and repetition are wonderful for learning.
Most babies this age are on a solid 2-nap schedule. Morning and afternoon naps with wake windows of 2.5-3.5 hours work well for many families.
Your baby may experience a sleep regression linked to big developmental leaps like crawling, pulling up, and separation anxiety. It will pass.
If your baby practices standing in the crib instead of sleeping, gently lay them down without making it a game. They'll figure it out soon.
Your baby may resist naps because there's so much to explore. A calm wind-down routine before each nap signals it's time to rest.
Night wakings due to separation anxiety are common now. A brief, boring check-in reassures your baby without fully waking them.
Total sleep is typically 12-16 hours in 24 hours at this age, including naps. If your baby sleeps on the lower end but seems rested and happy, that's fine.
If bedtime is becoming a battle, your baby might need a slightly later bedtime or more active play during the day to burn energy.

A lovey or comfort object can help with separation anxiety. Let your baby cuddle it during the wind-down routine, but always remove it from the crib before sleep — safe sleep guidelines recommend a bare crib until 12 months.
If your baby wakes early (before 6 AM), they may be overtired. Try an earlier bedtime — counterintuitively, it often leads to later wake-ups.
Keep the bedtime routine short and consistent: 20-30 minutes is plenty. A bath, book, song, and into the crib is a reliable formula.
If your baby still wakes to feed at night, they may not need the calories at this age. Gradually reducing night feeds can help them sleep through.
New teeth — like the upper front teeth or lateral incisors — may be coming in around this age and can cause extra fussiness at bedtime. A chilled teething ring before bed and extra comfort can help.
Avoid screen time close to bedtime. The stimulation can make it harder for your baby to wind down, even if the content seems calm.
If naps are getting shorter, try extending wake windows slightly. Sometimes an extra 15-20 minutes of awake time leads to better naps.
Daylight savings changes can be tough. Shift bedtime by 15 minutes each day over 3-4 days to ease the transition.

Solid foods are an exciting new world for your baby. Start with single foods and gradually build toward a variety of fruits, vegetables, grains, and proteins. By 8-9 months, many babies enjoy 2-3 small meals a day.
Encourage self-feeding with finger foods. Soft, bite-sized pieces of banana, avocado, sweet potato, or well-cooked pasta are great options.
Your baby can now eat most of what the family eats, just cut into safe sizes and without added salt or sugar. This simplifies meal prep!
Offer a variety of textures: mashed, soft chunks, and finger foods. Moving beyond purees helps develop chewing skills and prevents texture aversion later.
Breast milk or formula is still important, but solid food is taking on a bigger role in nutrition. Offer solids before milk at mealtimes if your baby is interested.
Picky eating can start emerging. Keep offering a variety of foods without pressure. Your job is to offer, your baby's job is to decide how much to eat.
Let your baby practice with a spoon, even if most food ends up on the floor. Pre-load a spoon and hand it to them to build independence.
Offer water with meals in an open cup or straw cup. Your baby needs small sips of water now that solids are a regular part of their diet.
Iron-rich foods remain important. Offer meat, beans, lentils, tofu, and iron-fortified cereals regularly to support your baby's rapid growth.
If your baby throws food on the floor, they may be done eating, experimenting with gravity, or telling you they don't want that food. It's all normal.
Avoid giving your baby juice. Whole fruits provide more fiber and less sugar. Water and milk are the best drink choices.
Yogurt and cheese are great calcium-rich foods for babies this age. Choose plain, full-fat varieties without added sugar.
Shared family mealtimes, even if your baby just plays with food, teach important social skills and make them more willing to try what others are eating.
If breastfeeding, your baby may start nursing less as they eat more solids. This is a natural transition and doesn't mean you need to wean.
Healthy fats are essential for brain development. Avocado, olive oil, nut butters (spread thin), and full-fat dairy are excellent sources.
Regular developmental checkups are important during this stage. Your pediatrician will assess motor skills, communication, and social interaction.
With your baby increasingly mobile, bumps and minor injuries become more common. Most are harmless, but watch for signs of concussion after head bumps.
Continue brushing emerging teeth twice a day with a tiny smear of fluoride toothpaste. This prevents early childhood cavities.
If your baby attends daycare, expect more colds and minor illnesses. Each one builds their immune system, even though it's hard to watch.
Hand-foot-and-mouth disease is common in babies and toddlers. Look for blisters on hands, feet, and in the mouth, along with fever. It's uncomfortable but usually resolves on its own.
Check with your pediatrician about whether your baby is up to date on vaccinations. Staying on schedule provides the best protection, and catch-up doses are available if any were missed.
Teething can cause drooling, fussiness, and a mild low-grade temperature, but a true fever (over {{100.4°F|38°C}}) isn't caused by teething. See your doctor if fever is present.
Lead exposure is a concern once babies are crawling and putting everything in their mouths. If you have an older home, ask about lead testing.
Your baby's pediatrician may check iron levels around 9-12 months. Iron deficiency can affect development, so mention it if you're concerned.
Roseola is common between 6-12 months: sudden high fever for a few days, then a rash appears as the fever breaks. It's alarming but usually harmless.
If your baby isn't babbling, making eye contact, or responding to their name by 9 months, bring it up with your pediatrician for an early evaluation.
Sun-protective clothing and shade are the best defenses against UV damage. For exposed skin, sunscreen is now safe for babies 6 months and older — choose a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher.

Bug bites are more common now that your baby spends time on the floor and outdoors. DEET-based repellents (up to 30% concentration) are safe at this age. You can also use mosquito nets and dress your baby in light long sleeves when outdoors.
If your baby has recurring ear infections, talk to your pediatrician about whether ear tubes might be worth considering.
Shoe-fitting isn't needed until your baby is walking outdoors regularly. For now, bare feet or non-slip socks give the best grip and sensory feedback for learning to stand.
Stack blocks and let your baby knock them down. As they get more skilled, they may start stacking one or two blocks themselves around 9-12 months.
Play "chase" by crawling after your baby or letting them crawl after you. This active game builds physical skills and is filled with giggles.
Offer containers with lids for your baby to practice opening and closing. Placing a toy inside gives them motivation to figure it out.
Read books with simple stories and let your baby turn the pages. Board books with flaps to lift add an interactive element they love.
Play "put in, take out" games with a bucket and balls or blocks. This in-and-out repetition is fascinating to babies and builds fine motor skills.
Try simple sorting activities: offer a muffin tin and different objects to place in each cup. Your baby is starting to notice categories and differences.
Water play at the sink or in a shallow basin with cups, spoons, and funnels is endlessly entertaining and teaches concepts like full, empty, and pour.
Sing action songs like "Itsy Bitsy Spider" or "Pat-a-Cake" with hand motions. Your baby may start trying to do the motions with you.
Create a safe climbing space with large cushions on the floor. Babies this age love to climb, and it builds strength, coordination, and confidence.
Push toys (that your baby pushes while walking) are wonderful for babies who are cruising. They provide support and motivation to take steps.

Toward the end of this stage, try offering a large, non-toxic crayon and paper. Your baby may bang it or mouth it at first, but with supervision they are starting to discover that tools can leave marks.
Play hide and seek by hiding behind a door and calling your baby's name. Their delight when they find you reinforces object permanence.
Offer toys with moving parts: doors that open, wheels that spin, buttons that click. These fine motor challenges are perfectly suited for this age.
Take your baby to a playground and let them experience the baby swing. The gentle motion and new environment are great sensory experiences.
Let your baby "help" with simple tasks like putting a washcloth in the laundry basket or placing a cup on the table. They love feeling included.
Now that your baby is pulling up on everything, re-check that all furniture is anchored to the wall. Dressers and bookshelves are the most common tip-over hazards.
Keep bathroom doors closed or use door handle covers. Toilets, tubs, and bathroom cabinets all pose risks to a curious crawler.
Stove knob covers and oven locks are important now. Your baby can reach higher than you expect, and hot surfaces cause serious burns.
Never leave small objects like coins, beads, or deflated balloons where your baby can reach them. Their improved pincer grasp means they can pick up very small items.
Keep your baby rear-facing in the car seat for as long as possible, until your child reaches the maximum height or weight allowed by the car seat manufacturer. Rear-facing is the safest position.
Check that your safety gates are securely installed. A determined baby can push against a poorly mounted gate and dislodge it.
Put door stops or door holders on doors that could slam on small fingers. Finger injuries from closing doors are very common at this age.
Keep trash cans covered or in locked cabinets. Babies are fascinated by garbage and may find dangerous items like sharp can lids or small packaging.
If you have a pet food or water bowl on the floor, move it to an area your baby can't access. Pet food is a choking hazard and water bowls are a drowning risk.
Secure appliance cords (toaster, kettle, lamp) so your baby can't pull them down. Wrapping excess cord and using cord covers helps.
Window guards or stops are essential, especially above the first floor. A screen alone won't prevent a baby from falling through an open window.
Be vigilant about older siblings' toys with small parts. Legos, marbles, and doll accessories are all choking hazards for a baby this age.
Store all medications, vitamins, and supplements in high, locked cabinets. Child-resistant caps slow kids down but don't stop them.
If your baby pulls up on the dishwasher door, use a dishwasher lock. Knives, forks, and detergent pods inside are serious hazards.
When your baby starts cruising, check that area rugs are secured with non-slip pads. Sliding rugs can cause falls on hard floors.
Your baby may start dropping objects on purpose and watching where they fall. This isn't naughty — it's a science experiment about gravity and cause and effect.
Try narrating your daily activities in simple words. "Now we're putting on your socks" builds vocabulary even before your baby can speak.
Your baby may start looking where you point instead of at your finger. This shared attention is a major cognitive milestone that supports language learning.
Offer your baby two toys at once when their hands are full. Figuring out how to hold a third item or set one down is real problem-solving in action.
Your baby's memory is growing fast. They may remember where a favorite toy is kept and crawl toward that spot, even if they can't see the toy.
If your baby has started crawling in their sleep and waking themselves up, give them plenty of crawling practice during the day so the novelty wears off.
A consistent wake-up time in the morning helps anchor your baby's entire day. Try to start the day within a 30-minute window, even on weekends.
If your baby fights the second nap, they may need a slightly longer wake window before it. Try adding 15 minutes of awake time and see if it helps.
Offering a small feeding or snack 30 minutes before bedtime can help your baby sleep more comfortably without creating a feed-to-sleep association.
If your baby only naps for 30 minutes, they may be waking between sleep cycles. Giving them a few minutes before going in can help them learn to connect cycles.
Try offering strips of soft food your baby can hold in their fist and gnaw on. Think steamed carrot sticks, ripe mango slices, or toast fingers.
If your baby gags on new textures, stay calm and give them time. Gagging is a safety reflex that helps them learn to manage food — it's not the same as choking.
Introducing spices and herbs like cinnamon, basil, and cumin is perfectly safe and helps your baby develop a varied palate early on.
If your baby suddenly refuses a food they used to enjoy, keep offering it without pressure. Taste preferences shift frequently at this age and often come back around.
Offering foods from your own plate (as long as they're safe and unsalted) can spark your baby's interest. They love eating what you're eating.

If your baby has a persistent cough at night, running a cool-mist humidifier in the room can bring relief. Never elevate or incline the crib mattress — babies need a firm, flat surface. See your pediatrician if the cough lasts more than a week.
Constipation can happen as your baby eats more solids. Offer water between meals and fiber-rich foods like prunes, pears, and peas to keep things moving.
Cradle cap sometimes returns or appears for the first time around this age. Gently massaging the scalp with oil and brushing with a soft brush usually resolves it.
If your baby's nose is constantly runny without other symptoms, it could be allergies rather than a cold. Mention it at your next pediatrician visit.
Your baby's rapid growth may cause mild bow-leggedness. This is completely normal at this age and typically straightens out on its own as they grow.
Try giving your baby a small basket of scarves or fabric scraps to pull out one by one. The colors and textures make it a wonderful sensory activity.
Make a simple shaker by putting dry pasta or rice inside a sealed container. Your baby will love shaking it and discovering the sounds they can create.
Try playing "where's the music?" by hiding a small musical toy under a blanket while it plays. Your baby will use their hearing to find it.
Tape a large piece of paper to the floor and let your baby explore finger painting with yogurt or baby-safe food coloring. It's messy but wonderful for sensory development.
Offer your baby a toy phone or remote control and pretend to have a conversation with them. This back-and-forth play builds early communication skills.
Check that houseplants are out of reach or non-toxic. Many common houseplants like pothos and philodendron can cause irritation or illness if chewed on.
Keep purses and bags off the floor. They often contain small items like coins, lip balm, pens, and medications that are dangerous for a curious baby.
Make sure the crib mattress is at its lowest setting now that your baby can pull up. A baby who can stand may be able to climb over a too-high mattress railing.
Refrigerator magnets are a hidden hazard — small ones can be swallowed. Move decorative magnets up high or remove them until your baby is older.
If you use a tablecloth, switch to placemats for now. Your baby can pull a tablecloth and bring hot food, dishes, or heavy objects down on themselves.
